elements.text:
Elin Strand, Head of Product
Tomas Reyes, Head of Platform

Leadership team and board
Review on 15 Dec 2026

pages.notes: Welcome. This is the plan for what Plumb builds in 2027, how we would staff it, and the three decisions we need from you at the end. Eighteen minutes, then questions.

elements.text: What Plumb builds in 2027, what we leave alone, and what we need to get there.

pages.notes: Seven parts. Part one is short: two slides on where the numbers stand. Most of the time goes on the roadmap and the bets.

elements.text: Teams adopt Plumb in a week and leave in a year.
Churned with "cannot see why builds are slow"

pages.notes: The product is easy to start and easy to outgrow. Almost six in ten of the teams that leave tell us the same thing: they cannot see why their builds are slow.
Growth is healthy. The third column is the one to watch: retention has slipped three points in a quarter, and builds are only slowly getting faster.

elements.text: Growth held through the March price change and stepped up when Pipelines launched in June.
Product analytics, weeks 45 of 2025 to 44 of 2026

pages.notes: Read this as a healthy line with one dent. The dent is the March price change; the step is the Pipelines launch. Neither changed the long term slope much, which is the point of the next slide.

elements.text: Three themes, ranked by what they do for retention.

pages.notes: Part two. Three themes, each tied to one number we can check next December.

elements.text: Every build shows where its time went, with no plugin to install.
Remote cache and test selection are on by default.
Roles, audit log and single sign on for teams past fifty.
Platform health is funded from each theme, not a fourth line.

pages.notes: Each theme has one customer visible change and one number. If we cannot measure it in December, we should not have built it.
Solid bars are committed, outlined bars are exploring and can move. The one date we defend is remote cache going general availability at the end of June.

elements.text:
A cache that works
without setup
fallback: direct upload when the edge is down

pages.notes: The cache moves from something a customer configures to something they never notice. The new part is the edge: it answers from the nearest of twelve regions, so a hash check costs under 40 milliseconds.
Impact is our estimate of net retention points, effort is engineer months. Three bets clear the bar for the first half: the cache, the timeline and single sign on.

elements.text: Twelve engineers today, sixteen from the second quarter. Effort moves from theme A to theme C as the year goes on.
A  Know why it is slow

pages.notes: Four hires land by the end of the second quarter, two in February and two in April. Without them the cache and single sign on cannot both ship in the first half.

elements.text: Cut test selection first, keep the ship date.
Cloud cost rises with cache traffic
Tiered storage and a 30 day expiry.
Two senior hires take until Q3
Two contractors lined up from February.
Large customers need SSO by April
Pull SSO forward as a beta in March.

pages.notes: R4 is the one that needs a decision: two of our largest customers have asked for single sign on before April, so we propose a beta in March.

elements.text: We stopped arguing about whose change broke the build. The timeline just shows it.

pages.notes: One of twelve customer interviews we ran in September. It is typical: the value is that the argument ends, not that the build gets faster.

elements.text: Two start in February, two in April. Backfills are not included.
Cloud budget for twelve regions through the first year.
Cache v2, build timeline and SSO. Everything else can move.

pages.notes: The ask in one slide. Four hires, a cloud budget for the cache edge, and a decision by the fifteenth of December so the February hires can start on time.
Open the floor. Backup material, including the metric definitions and the full risk register, is in the shared folder.

elements.text: How long a mobile checkout can make people wait before they leave
K. Hallin, J. Mbeki, S. Ito

pages.notes: This is the report from our spring study on waiting at checkout. The ruler is the whole story: the orange stretch, five to eight seconds, is where people leave.

elements.text: How long can a checkout make a person wait before they leave?
Leaving rises smoothly with every extra second.
Older people tolerate a wait longer than younger ones.
A progress bar changes what people do.

pages.notes: One question, three hypotheses. We wrote them down before the first participant, which matters for the next slides: one of them turned out to be wrong.

elements.text: Remote, 12 March to 4 June 2026, median session 14 minutes
612 Swedish adults from a consumer panel, all on their own phone.
Buy a train ticket in a working prototype.
A wait of one to eight seconds at the payment step.
Completed or left, time, and a trust rating from 1 to 7.

pages.notes: Each person saw one condition only, so nobody could compare waits. The delay sat at the payment step because that is where a real checkout calls the bank.
The sample leans slightly to 30 to 44 year olds, which mirrors who buys train tickets on a phone. Everyone was on a phone, mostly on mobile data.

elements.text:
At five and eight seconds, half of each group
also saw a progress bar.
Seconds of added wait at the payment step

pages.notes: The four bars are the four conditions, drawn to the same scale as the ruler on the cover. The eight second wait is long on purpose: we wanted to see where people break.
Five findings. The first two are about when people leave, the next two about who and what helps, and the last one is about trust.

elements.text: Nothing happens until 2.5 seconds, then people start to leave
Overall, 121 of 612 people left before paying: one in five.

pages.notes: H1 said leaving would rise smoothly. It did not. One second and two and a half seconds are statistically the same; the damage starts after that.

elements.text: Going from 2.5 to 5 seconds multiplied the chance of leaving by two and a half.
153 people in each condition, the threshold sits between 2.5 and 5 seconds

pages.notes: The two groups are the same size, so the comparison is clean. We report the odds ratio in the appendix; the headline is the plain ratio of the two rates.

elements.text: At the eight second wait, the share who abandoned, with 95 percent intervals.

pages.notes: This was a surprise. H2 predicted older people would wait longer; the data say younger people leave sooner, though the oldest group is small, which is why its interval is wide.

elements.text: A progress bar took 16 points off the worst wait.
At eight seconds: 38 of 77 left without it, 25 of 76 with it. At five seconds the gap was 9 points.

pages.notes: H3 held. The progress bar changed nothing about the wait, only what people believed was happening, and it recovered about a third of the people we would have lost.

elements.text: Mean trust in the shop, rated from 1 to 7 after the task. Whiskers show 95 percent intervals.
Even among people who paid, an eight second wait cost 1.7 points.

pages.notes: Trust is the quiet result. Five seconds already costs about eight tenths of a point, well before most people have left. The ones who stay just trust the shop less.

elements.text: Two and a half seconds is free. Five is where the cost starts.
Patience is not the variable. Young people leave faster than old ones.
Showing progress wins back about a third of the people a long wait would lose.
Trust moves before behaviour does. Five seconds already costs eight tenths of a point.

pages.notes: These are the four sentences we would want a product team to remember from the whole study. Each one points back to a finding.

elements.text:
If you run a checkout, spend the first seconds
freely and stop at five.
Spend it on work people cannot see: validation and fraud checks.
Show progress as soon as the wait passes 2.5 seconds. Do not wait to be asked.
Do not ship it. Split the step, or move the work out of the payment path.
Budget two seconds a step. Show progress at 2.5. Stop at 5.

pages.notes: The practical version of the whole study. Three zones on one ruler. If a step cannot finish inside five seconds, the fix is in the design of the step, not in a faster spinner.

elements.text: What this does not tell you
Buying a train ticket in a prototype. Other purchases may differ.
Real sites jitter. We did not test a slow start with a fast finish.
Swedish adults with a recent phone. No one on an old handset.
Variable waits, mixed in one session
Waits that change within a session, the way real pages behave. Recruiting from January.

pages.notes: Three honest limits. We are running a follow up in spring that mixes slow and fast steps in a single session, because real checkouts do that.

elements.text: Intervals are Wilson 95 %. Trust is the mean of a 1 to 7 rating.

pages.notes: The full table behind every chart. Intervals are Wilson intervals. Trust is the mean of a one to seven rating.

elements.text:
Ines Carvalho, platform engineer
Nordkvist, Stockholm

A laptop with Docker
and a pot of strong coffee

pages.notes: Welcome. Ninety minutes: 25 of ideas, 40 of building, a live demo and a short wrap. The dots on the right are the whole talk: waiting longer each time you try again.

elements.text: Delivery, keys and backoff, drawn out.
Build the whole thing in five steps.

pages.notes: The bar is drawn to scale. Most of the evening is the lab, because nobody remembers a diagram until they have broken it themselves.

elements.text: A retry is a promise to do the same thing twice.
So the second time has to be as safe as the first. Everything in the next ninety minutes follows from that.

pages.notes: Say the sentence slowly. Everything we build tonight is about making the second attempt as safe as the first one.

elements.text: At least once, never exactly once
A queue promises the job arrives. It cannot promise it arrives once.

Job 41 ran twice.
Both runs were correct.
That is the problem.

pages.notes: Walk the numbers. One: send. Two: deliver. Three: the consumer finishes but its acknowledgement is lost. Four: the queue waits thirty seconds. Five: it delivers again. The consumer has now done the work twice.

elements.text: A key makes the second run harmless
The caller picks the key once and sends it with every attempt.
Sent as a header with every attempt

pages.notes: The decision diamond is the whole idea. If we have seen the key, we hand back the saved reply and do no work. If not, we do the work and save the reply under the key.

elements.text: Twelve clients fail together and retry on a doubling clock.

Five walls of
twelve at once.

pages.notes: Both panels show the same twelve clients. Without jitter the retries land in five identical walls and knock the server over again. With jitter the same retries are spread out.
Laptops open now. Pull the repo from the link on the last slide, or follow along on the projector and do it later.

elements.text: Each step is small enough to test on its own. Do them in this order.
Build the key from the order id and the action, never a random value.
Insert a row with the key before anything else happens.
Run it in the same transaction as the insert.
Save the reply next to the key for 24 hours.
A replay returns the saved body
Ack the message only after the commit succeeds.

pages.notes: Five steps, in this order. The last one matters most: acknowledge only after the commit. People often do it first and lose jobs instead of doubling them.
At least once with an idempotency key behaves like exactly once from the outside. That is the third column, and it is what the lab builds.

elements.text: Duplicate charges per month, before and after

pages.notes: This is Nordkvist in production over six months. Eleven duplicate charges a month became none. The price was 38 milliseconds on the slowest path.

elements.text: If the demo gods say no, there is a recorded run at the end of the deck.
worker killed in the middle of a job

pages.notes: Four commands. Flood the queue with five hundred jobs, kill the worker in the middle, and let the report count what happened. The line to point at is the last one: zero applied twice.

elements.text: Key on the order, not the clock.
Add jitter before you add capacity.

pages.notes: Four lines to remember. If the audience keeps only one, make it the last: acknowledge last.

elements.text: Scan for the slides and the lab

pages.notes: Everything is at the first link. The two papers are short and worth reading; the Brooker post is the one that made me add jitter in the first place.
Tack. Questions here or at the bar. I am at the office every Thursday if you want to look at your own queue together.
